$comment: AI ships at sea (PRD sections 4 and 6). About 'population' ships sail at once, by role share (the famous pirates, pirates.json, sail over and above it). A merchant buys at most voyageUnits a voyage, and only while the far port pays minMargin over its price; no more than maxPerRoute sail the same port pair at once. They skim a trade rather than flood it, so prices move without the player's routes drying up (checked by a route probe). Seeing is by the weather (sightByWind for the wind where the player is, closing to stormSight in a storm, times nightSight after dark). viewTiles times it (viewTiles() in @corsair/data) is how far she can make out a ship on the sea: the 3D view's haze lies on that horizon and ships are drawn that far, a click or a hover finds them, I intercepts the nearest, AI fights within it play out on the map for her to join (and she hears their guns), and the sea brings new ships and staged fights in from beyond it. sightTiles times it (sightTiles()) is her lookouts' sight: what the chart and minimap remember. Hailing works within hailTiles. Lanes are found on a grid of laneCell x laneCell tiles; each ship keeps her own line up to laneSpreadTiles to one side of a lane, so ships sharing it sail side by side; beating to windward, she tacks in boards up to tackTiles off it. Ships lie in port portDays before sailing on. A new ship tops up the sea from a port out of the player's sight, so none appears at a quay she is watching. Pirates mark ports near their haven (by size, interest halving at pirateRangeTiles) and lie in wait lurkDays on the lane, cruising slow circles on watch meanwhile (lurkSail: so far a second, so many degrees a second; a ship lying dead still at sea looks broken). Convoys (PRD section 6, slice 2): each line sails on a timetable (every everyDays from firstDay): from the Atlantic entry off the map's east edge (or from a port, for the treasure ship) to one of its ports in turn, bringing goods and settlers (people: a share of the port's people), then loading what it takes and sailing home. Its coming is news. Merchants never call at the ports of a nation at war with theirs. A patrol at war sails to blockade an enemy port with chance blockade.chance (the nearer the likelier, interest halving by blockade.rangeTiles, and at most blockade.maxPerPort to a port), lying within blockade.tiles for blockade.days, beating to and fro across its approach up to blockade.beatTiles each way, and daring its guns to take what goes in or out; otherwise patrols head for their ports where merchants have been lost in the last patrolLosses.days days. Each role draws her class from 'classes' by weight (her own stream, so the draw moves nothing else); the debug spawn sails the role's classId. A pirate sails biggerPirates.classId instead at odds rising to its maxShare as the player's strength (crew x (1 + guns/10)) grows from 'from' to 'full'. Convoys sail merchantmen, the Spanish flota a galleon, the treasure ship a treasure galleon. Danger (slice 2 of docs/design/combat-model.md): each sea area has a tier, 1 quiet (the Caribbean Sea, the Lesser Antilles) to 4 the treasure routes (the Gulf of Mexico); a pirate marks ports in waters that fit her ship's rung ('danger.classRung'), so sloops haunt the quiet coasts and brigantines the Main; the HUD names the waters' tier. Fits (slice 5): each AI ship carries the shipwright's upgrades by her role, each at its chance in 'fits' (navy planking and bronze, pirates copper and swivels, merchants nettings), so a well-fitted prize is worth more. Ships (slice 7): a role's 'byNation' adds classes to the mix for that nation's ships (Spain's guarda costa half-galleys, England's galley-frigate); pirates sail pinnaces and periaguas too, and merchants ketches and pinks.
